note: News told at a trading counter (ASK FOR NEWS). Information only: no rule reads this file, so it is not part of the rules fingerprint.
sources: Joseph Meek reached St. Joseph on 4 May 1848 with word of the Whitman killings (Oregon Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, Joseph Meek).
The ship Honolulu reached Portland in summer 1848, buying tools with California gold dust (Offbeat Oregon, H023).
Paris revolution news was in New York by late March 1848 (Michigan Liberty Press, 13 April 1848).
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo: signed 2 February, ratified by the Senate 10 March, proclaimed 4 July 1848. Oregon Territory Act signed 14 August 1848.
Road notes follow Joel Palmer's 1847 journal and NPS Oregon Trail narratives already cited in route.json.

headlines.text: General Scott's army holds Mexico City. Commissioners are talking peace with the Mexican government.
The Senate has ratified the peace treaty with Mexico. California and New Mexico are to be ceded to the United States for fifteen million dollars.
Steamer news from Europe: King Louis Philippe has fled Paris and France is a republic again. People say risings are spreading to the German states.
Joe Meek came through from Oregon on his way to Washington. Dr. Whitman, his wife and a dozen others were killed at Waiilatpu last November, and Oregon volunteers are fighting the Cayuse.
Colonel Gilliam of the Oregon volunteers is dead, accidentally shot in camp on his way back to The Dalles. The volunteers have built a fort at the burned mission.
The Democrats met in Baltimore and nominated General Lewis Cass of Michigan for President.
Wisconsin has been admitted to the Union as the thirtieth state.
Brigham Young is bringing the main body of the Mormons from Winter Quarters to the Salt Lake this season. Their trains keep to the north bank of the Platte.
Lieutenant Woodbury and a company of soldiers are building a new army post at the head of Grand Island on the Platte.
The Whigs met in Philadelphia and nominated General Zachary Taylor, the hero of Buena Vista.
Word from the Salt Lake: crickets came down on the Mormon wheat this spring, and flocks of gulls ate them.
Peace with Mexico was proclaimed on the Fourth of July. The regiments are coming home.
Most of the Oregon volunteers have gone home to their farms. A small garrison still holds Waiilatpu, and the Cayuse who did the killing are not taken.
A ship came up the Columbia buying every pick and shovel in Portland with gold dust. They say gold lies loose in the streams of California, and many men in Oregon are talking of going south.
A new Free Soil party met at Buffalo and nominated Martin Van Buren, against carrying slavery into the new territories.
Congress has made Oregon a territory of the United States, with slavery barred there. Oregon will have a governor appointed from Washington.
The New York papers print letters from California about gold on the American River. Most people back home think it is a tall tale.
General Taylor has won the election for President.

road.elm_grove: Only a stump or two is left at Elm Grove. Campers have cut every tree, so carry wood from the last creek.
road.wakarusa: The banks of the Wakarusa are steep. Teams let the wagons down with ropes.
road.kansas_river: The Kansas is too deep to ford for most of the season. Ferrymen take wagons over for pay.
road.big_blue: The Big Blue rises fast after rain. Some trains have waited days at the ford for it to fall.
road.platte: Once you strike the Platte the road runs level for weeks. There is little wood, so gather buffalo chips for the fires.
road.fort_kearny: Soldiers are camped at the head of Grand Island this summer. There is no store there yet.
road.south_platte: The South Platte ford is wide and shallow over quicksand. Keep the teams moving, or the wheels settle into the sand.
road.ash_hollow: The road drops into Ash Hollow down a steep hill. Lock the wheels and let the wagons down on ropes. There is good spring water and ash wood at the bottom.
road.courthouse_rock: Courthouse Rock stands off the road to the south. It looks closer than it is.
road.chimney_rock: You will see Chimney Rock for two or three days before you pass it.
road.scotts_bluff: The road leaves the river and goes around the bluffs to the south. Water is scarce on that stretch.
road.fort_laramie: Fort Laramie belongs to the American Fur Company. Prices there are high, and many trains lighten their wagons before the hills.
road.north_platte: The Mormons run a ferry at the upper crossing of the North Platte. Fording there is dangerous in high water.
road.independence_rock: Between the North Platte and the Sweetwater the springs are poisoned with alkali. Do not let the cattle drink.
road.devils_gate: The Sweetwater runs through a cleft in the rock at Devil's Gate. The road goes around it.
road.south_pass: The climb to South Pass is so gentle that you hardly notice the summit. The nights are cold even in July.
road.little_sandy: After Pacific Springs the water is scarce. Fill every keg and canteen.
road.green_river: The Green is swift and deep. Ferrymen work the southern crossing and charge more when the river is up.
road.greenwood_cutoff: Greenwood's Cutoff saves days but crosses about forty miles without water. Travel by night and carry water and grass.
road.fort_bridger: Bridger and Vasquez keep a small post with a blacksmith. There is not much to buy there.
road.soda_springs: At Soda Springs the water bubbles out of the ground and tastes like soda. It is good drinking.
road.fort_hall: Fort Hall belongs to the Hudson's Bay Company. They sell flour, but it is dear.
road.snake_river: Down the Snake the road keeps above the canyon, and the river is often out of reach below the cliffs. The grass is poor.
road.fort_boise: Fort Boise is a small Hudson's Bay post. The road crosses the Snake again near it, and the ford is deep.
road.burnt_river: The Burnt River canyon is the roughest road yet. It crosses and recrosses the creek all day.
road.powder_river: The Powder River valley has fair grass. Rest the teams there if you can.
road.grande_ronde: The Grande Ronde is a fine valley with good grass and water. Rest the teams there before the Blue Mountains.
road.blue_mountains: The road over the Blue Mountains is steep and heavily timbered. Snow can come by the end of September.
road.umatilla: The road comes down to the Umatilla. Since the Whitman killings the Cayuse country is unsettled, so travel in company.
road.fort_walla_walla: The Hudson's Bay post at Walla Walla stays out of the war. Oregon volunteers hold the burned mission at Waiilatpu.
road.john_day: The road follows the Columbia west over sand and rock. There is little grass.
road.deschutes: Indians at the Deschutes ferry goods across in canoes for pay. Swim the stock over.
road.the_dalles: At The Dalles you choose between the Barlow Road over the Cascades, which charges a toll, and rafting down the Columbia.
road.columbia_raft: The Cascades of the Columbia cannot be run. Everything must be portaged around them.
road.barlow_pass: The Barlow Road climbs through heavy timber south of Mount Hood. Cut grass for the stock where you find it.
road.laurel_hill: Laurel Hill is so steep that wagons are let down on ropes snubbed around the trees.
road.eagle_creek: Philip Foster's farm at Eagle Creek sells flour and beef to people coming off the Barlow Road.
road.oregon_city: Oregon City sits at the falls of the Willamette. Food is dear there after the war.
